title: Data Types — typing drills
description: Type short GDScript for strings, bools, arrays, dictionaries, and a null check. Quotes and spacing can vary; a trailing semicolon is fine.

drills.prompt: Declare a String variable named current_room set to Basement.
drills.hint: Text values need quotes around them, and the line starts with var.
drills.explain: Without quotes, Godot would think Basement is a name, not text. Single or double quotes both work in GDScript.

drills.prompt: Declare a bool named is_flashlight_on set to false.
drills.hint: A bool is just true or false, written in lowercase, with no quotes.
drills.explain: is_flashlight_on is a yes-or-no flag. false means the beam starts off.

drills.prompt: Declare a typed array of strings named inventory that starts with flashlight and key, in that order.
drills.hint: Use square brackets. Array[String] is the typed form, and indexes will start at 0.
drills.explain: inventory[0] is "flashlight" and inventory[1] is "key". Typing the array as Array[String] helps Godot catch mistakes early.

drills.prompt: Declare a dictionary named stats with fear set to 0.0 and stamina set to 100.0.
drills.hint: A dictionary uses curly braces and labeled values, like "fear": 0.0.
drills.explain: A dictionary is a tiny filing cabinet of labeled values. You can also write Godot's identifier form, {fear = 0.0, stamina = 100.0}.

drills.prompt: Write the if line that checks whether monster is not null.
drills.hint: Start with if, compare monster to null, and end the line with a colon.
drills.explain: null means nothing is here yet. Checking if monster != null: before you use it stops the game from crashing when a creature has not been spawned.
